my_sentence: I send my family to Beijing to join a speech, and then I backed to home.
correction: I sent my family to Beijing to attend a speech, and then I came back home.
explanation: Use past tense for the completed trip: "sent" and "came back." The natural collocation is "attend a speech."
correct_examples: I sent my children to Beijing and came back home.
They attended a speech yesterday.

my_sentence: Every year my country has different speech for children.
correction: Every year my country has different speeches for children.
explanation: The statement refers to multiple events in different places or years, so use the plural count noun "speeches."
correct_examples: The school organizes several speeches every year.
Different speeches are held for children.

my_sentence: You need to go to the city to get some opportunities and then to province.
correction: You need to go to the city to get some opportunities, and then to the province.
explanation: Use the article "the" before the specific administrative region being discussed.
correct_examples: They went to the city and then to the province.
She moved from the city to the province.
context: Describing the stages of a competition.

my_sentence: It is just to help your children improve speaking skills in public.
correction: It is just to help your children improve their speaking skills in public.
explanation: Use the possessive determiner "their" before "speaking skills" because the skills belong to the children.
correct_examples: The course helps students improve their speaking skills.
Practice can improve their confidence in public.
context: Explaining the purpose of the speech event.

my_sentence: It's an opportunity to Beijing to have a vacation.
correction: It's an opportunity to go to Beijing for a vacation.
explanation: Use "opportunity to go to + place" and "for a vacation" to express the purpose of the trip.
correct_examples: It was an opportunity to go to Beijing.
We went there for a short vacation.
context: Explaining an extra benefit of the trip.

my_sentence: They coming back next week.
correction: They are coming back next week.
explanation: The present continuous requires the auxiliary verb "are" before the -ing form.
correct_examples: They are coming back on Friday.
My family is coming home next week.
context: Saying when the family will return.

my_sentence: The speech lasts four days.
correction: The speech lasts for four days.
explanation: Use "last for + duration" when stating how long an event continues.
correct_examples: The conference lasts for three days.
The course lasts for six weeks.
context: Describing the length of the event.

my_sentence: Most of them are international and domesticated.
correction: Most of them are international and domestic.
explanation: "Domestic" is the adjective meaning within one country; "domesticated" normally describes animals made tame.
correct_examples: The competition has domestic and international events.
They serve both domestic and overseas customers.

my_sentence: If you just stay your city, you can't meet a lot of people.
correction: If you just stay in your city, you can't meet a lot of people.
explanation: Use the preposition "in" with the verb "stay" before a place.
correct_examples: If you stay in your city, you may miss opportunities.
She stayed in her hometown.
context: Explaining why competitions are held in different places.

my_sentence: Especially some of them are talented.
correction: Especially those who are talented.
explanation: Use a relative clause with "those who" when identifying people with a particular quality.
correct_examples: We invited those who were talented.
Students who work hard can advance.
context: Explaining whom students can meet at competitions.

my_sentence: The first prize is a iPad.
correction: The first prize is an iPad.
explanation: Use "an" before "iPad" because its spoken name begins with a vowel sound.
correct_examples: She won an iPad.
The prize was an iPhone.

my_sentence: If the government gives too much responsibilities to rich people, they may leave.
correction: If the government gives too many responsibilities to rich people, they may leave.
explanation: "Responsibilities" is a plural count noun, so use "many," not the uncountable quantifier "much."
correct_examples: Too many responsibilities can discourage investors.
The manager gave me too many tasks.
context: Discussing how government policy may affect wealthy people.

my_sentence: Finally it will reduce our economic.
correction: Finally, it will reduce our economy.
explanation: "Economy" is the noun for a country's financial system; "economic" is an adjective.
correct_examples: The policy could damage the economy.
A weak economy can reduce employment.
context: Discussing the possible effect of heavy responsibilities.

my_sentence: People may try to stay at home and don't lose anything.
correction: People may try to stay at home and not lose anything.
explanation: After "try to," coordinate the two infinitive verbs: "to stay ... and not lose."
correct_examples: They try to save money and not waste it.
He stayed home and did not spend anything.
context: Explaining why people might avoid becoming wealthy.

my_sentence: If I try to a new industry, everything is new for me.
correction: If I try to enter a new industry, everything will be new for me.
explanation: The verb needs an object such as "enter," and the result of the future condition uses "will be."
correct_examples: If I enter a new industry, I will need new skills.
Everything will be new when she changes careers.

my_sentence: This job have a higher threshold.
correction: This job has a higher threshold.
explanation: The singular subject "this job" takes "has," not "have."
correct_examples: This job has strict requirements.
The position has a high entry barrier.
context: Explaining why specialized jobs pay more.

my_sentence: If there are a lot of people who are poor and at the same time a lot of rich, they don't spend money to help.
correction: If there are a lot of poor people and, at the same time, a lot of rich people, they don't spend money to help.
explanation: Use the noun "people" after both adjectives to make the two groups clear.
correct_examples: There are many poor people and some rich people.
The rich and the poor have different needs.

my_sentence: That can make our society mess up.
correction: That can make our society become messy.
explanation: Use the adjective "messy" after "become" to describe the resulting condition.
correct_examples: Corruption can make society messy.
The conflict made the situation chaotic.

my_sentence: Some celebrities can use their influence to encourage the poor to use their weapon or power to hurt the rich.
correction: Some celebrities can use their influence to encourage poor people to use weapons or power to hurt the rich.
explanation: Use plural nouns for weapons in a general statement, and use "poor people" when referring to the group in general.
correct_examples: Celebrities can influence poor people.
People should not use weapons to hurt others.

my_sentence: I lived a countryside.
correction: I lived in the countryside.
explanation: The fixed phrase is "live in the countryside"; use the preposition "in" and the article "the."
correct_examples: I grew up in the countryside.
They live in the countryside.

my_sentence: I couldn't know a rich person.
correction: I had never met a rich person.
explanation: Use the verb "meet" for personal experience; the past perfect emphasizes that this had not happened during childhood.
correct_examples: I had never met anyone famous before.
She had never met a wealthy person.
context: Explaining why he did not hate rich people as a child.

my_sentence: They can receive many feedbacks and likes.
correction: They can receive a lot of feedback and likes.
explanation: "Feedback" is generally uncountable, so use "a lot of feedback" rather than plural "feedbacks."
correct_examples: The video received a lot of feedback.
She got positive feedback and many likes.

my_sentence: Some food and water are more expensive than their yearly salary.
correction: Some foods and water cost more than their yearly salary.
explanation: Use the plural count noun "foods" for different types of food, and use "cost more than" for a price comparison.
correct_examples: Some foods cost more than a day's wages.
Food and water can cost more than expected.
context: Discussing poor people's reaction to luxury consumption.

my_sentence: A lot of company started from scratch.
correction: A lot of companies have started from scratch.
explanation: After "a lot of," use the plural noun "companies"; the present perfect describes companies that have done this over time.
correct_examples: Many companies have started from scratch.
Several successful businesses began with one person.

my_sentence: They produce storage, memory, GPU and others.
correction: They produce storage devices, memory, GPUs, and other hardware.
explanation: Use plural forms for multiple products and name the category with the uncountable noun "hardware."
correct_examples: The company produces GPUs and other hardware.
They make memory and storage devices.

my_sentence: For most AI company in my country, they can't buy GPUs from Nvidia.
correction: For most AI companies in my country, they can't buy GPUs from Nvidia.
explanation: Use the plural noun "companies" after "most."
correct_examples: Most AI companies need powerful GPUs.
Most companies cannot buy directly from the manufacturer.

my_sentence: You can't find the difference the AI videos and real videos.
correction: You can't find the difference between AI videos and real videos.
explanation: The noun "difference" takes the preposition "between" when comparing two things.
correct_examples: Can you see the difference between the two images?
There is a clear difference between the products.

my_sentence: If someone want to use my face, they need to get permission from me.
correction: If someone wants to use my face, they need to get permission from me.
explanation: The singular indefinite pronoun "someone" takes the third-person singular verb "wants."
correct_examples: If someone wants to use my photo, they must ask me.
Someone wants to speak with you.
context: Discussing consent for AI face data.

my_sentence: Nowadays in my country we have some large to limit AI usage.
correction: Nowadays in my country we have some laws to limit AI usage.
explanation: The intended noun is plural "laws," not the adjective-like word "large."
correct_examples: The government passed laws to regulate AI.
These laws limit how companies use data.

my_sentence: It is so easier to manage.
correction: It is easier to manage.
explanation: Do not use the intensifier "so" directly before a comparative adjective in this structure; use "much easier" if stronger emphasis is needed.
correct_examples: The new system is easier to manage.
This process is much easier now.
context: Comparing work with and without AI.

my_sentence: Nowadays you can finish your tasks indeed, then using AI.
correction: Nowadays you can finish your tasks more easily by using AI.
explanation: Use the adverb "easily" to describe how the task is completed, and use "by using" to show the method.
correct_examples: You can work more efficiently by using AI.
She finished the task more easily with this tool.

my_sentence: AI can help you make your tasks more creativity.
correction: AI can help you make your tasks more creative.
explanation: After the linking verb "make + object," use the adjective "creative," not the noun "creativity."
correct_examples: The tool makes the design more creative.
This feature helps us produce more creative work.
